nameStory: Sea lettuce gets its name from its striking resemblance to the leafy green we toss in our salads! These thin, translucent green sheets rippling in the tide pools look remarkably like lettuce leaves floating in water. The comparison is so apt that this seaweed is actually edible and has been harvested as a nutritious sea vegetable for centuries.
description: Broadleaf Sea Lettuce is a bright green marine algae that grows as thin, flat sheets along New England's rocky shores. These translucent green "leaves" can range from small hand-sized patches to larger sheets up to a foot across. The algae feels slippery and delicate when wet, almost like wet tissue paper, and often has a wrinkled or ruffled appearance as it moves with the waves. You'll find it attached to rocks in tide pools and shallow coastal waters.

idTips.label: Thin translucent sheets
idTips.description: The algae forms paper-thin, see-through green sheets that you can easily hold up to the light - they're only two cells thick and feel delicate like wet tissue paper

idTips.label: Bright lettuce-green color
idTips.description: Vibrant, fresh green color that's unmistakably similar to garden lettuce, staying bright even when wet

idTips.label: Smooth, slippery texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and slippery when wet, with a soft texture that tears easily if pulled - much more delicate than leathery brown seaweeds

idTips.label: Irregular torn edges
idTips.description: Edges are often ragged and torn-looking from wave action, giving it a natural lettuce-leaf appearance rather than perfectly smooth borders

idTips.label: Fresh ocean scent
idTips.description: Smells like fresh ocean water with a clean, slightly briny aroma - not fishy or pungent like some seaweeds

habitat: Look for Broadleaf Sea Lettuce in tide pools and on rocks in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastline. It thrives in areas that are regularly covered and uncovered by tides, attaching to granite ledges, barnacle-covered rocks, and pier pilings. You'll often find it growing alongside rockweed and Irish moss in the middle to lower tide pool zones where it gets plenty of wave action.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins to appear as water temperatures warm, with fresh bright green sheets emerging on rocks. This is when sea lettuce is at its most tender and vibrant.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the largest, most abundant sheets visible during low tides. The algae is thick and lush, covering tide pool rocks in bright green carpets.
seasonality.fall: Still present and identifiable, though some sheets may show signs of aging with slightly duller color or more torn edges from summer storms.
seasonality.winter: Much reduced but still present in protected areas. Look for smaller, tougher sheets that have survived the harsh winter storms and cold water temperatures.

funFact: Sea lettuce is one of the few seaweeds that can actually survive in space! NASA has used it in experiments because it can tolerate extreme conditions and even produce oxygen in zero gravity - making it a potential food source for future Mars missions.
confusionNotes: Sea lettuce is most commonly confused with green plastic bags or debris floating in tide pools, especially when it's very translucent. The key difference is that real sea lettuce will be firmly attached to rocks and feel organic and slippery, while plastic feels artificial and often floats freely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sea lettuce,' this isn't actually a plant at all - it's a type of algae that lacks true roots, stems, or leaves. The 'broadleaf' in its name distinguishes it from other sea lettuces that grow as tubes or ribbons, making the naming a bit confusing since it's the classic sheet-like form most people picture when they hear 'sea lettuce.'
compareHints: Broadleaf Sea Lettuce differs from its relatives by forming broad, flat sheets rather than tubes or ribbons. Gutweed forms hollow green tubes that look like intestines, while Green String Lettuce grows as narrow ribbon-like strips. Thread Weed appears as thin, compressed strands rather than the wide, lettuce-like sheets of this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its flat relative Broadleaf Sea Lettuce which looks like green tissue paper, gutweed forms distinctive hollow tubes.
Green String Lettuce differs from Broadleaf Sea Lettuce by its narrow ribbon shape rather than broad, flat sheets.
Thread Weed differs from Broadleaf Sea Lettuce by being much narrower and more compressed rather than broad and flat.
